app: Render-tap feasibility on macOS (targets: TextEdit as a system/platform binary, Google Chrome as a hardened third-party app)

stack_detection.method: system policy + code-signing flags read before attempting anything
stack_detection.signature: csrutil status = enabled; Chrome CodeDirectory flags=0x12a00 (kill, restrict, library-validation, runtime); TextEdit is a platform binary under /System

channel_setup: The Linux reference cell taps GTK4's render tree by injecting a shim (LD_PRELOAD) plus a gdb tap on gsk_renderer_render. The macOS equivalent would require loading code into a third-party process (DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES) or attaching a debugger to it. Tested with a NO-OP probe dylib whose only action is appending one line to a log file — it hooks nothing; the question asked is purely whether the OS lets an outside library load at all.

t1_read_text.detail: Unreachable: no code can be loaded into the target to observe its render tree.

measurements.notes: MEASURED, with a positive control so the negative means something. (a) Control — the same probe dylib inserted into a locally compiled, unsigned binary: LOADS (1 log line). The mechanism works when nothing blocks it. (b) TextEdit (platform binary, /System, SIP-protected): 0 log lines — refused. (c) Google Chrome (hardened runtime + library-validation + restrict): 0 log lines — refused. So the exact policies that close this channel are: System Integrity Protection for Apple's own binaries, and the hardened runtime's library-validation flag (0x12a00) for third-party apps — the latter is chosen by the DEVELOPER, not by Apple, and is required for notarization in practice. No attempt was made to disable SIP or to work around either policy: the refusal IS the result. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PAPER: the channel that on Linux gives the strongest guarantee (the render tree cannot lie — it is what will be drawn, by construction) is structurally unavailable on macOS for every app that matters. What remains is the OS-mediated view: the Accessibility API, which is a semantic tree the app CHOOSES to publish. That is why macOS is the OS where 'only the platform vendor can provide this channel' is not an argument but an observation — and it is also why the AT-latch, the thin-tree risk and the annotation-quality question dominate every other macOS cell.

runtime_verification.method: positive control (unsigned local binary) vs two protected targets, identical probe dylib, marker-file presence as the discriminator
runtime_verification.agreement: n/a (blocked) — but the control proves the test itself is sound

permissions_required: none attempted beyond a normal user session; SIP left enabled throughout
